notes.4: In this question, candidates were asked to evaluate the view that personal data from digital technology should remain private and never be used by other people and organisations. Candidates were expected to justify their views using material drawn from the sources as well as their own experience and evidence. There were many thoughtful, well-explained discussions of arguments for and against the view in the statement, thereby exploring different perspectives on the issue. Most candidates explored issues of: • Data security • Theft of identity • Digital crime • Rights to privacy • Convenience and targeting of information and advertising • Tracking location in emergencies • Supporting research and innovation, e.g. in medical research • Help in finding information and products. Responses at the highest levels tended to have well supported, logical reasoning and make clear judgements about the issue. A clear, balanced assessment or conclusion was also reached. These responses linked their argument back to the issue in the statement. Weaker responses tended to be generalised, lack relevance to the issue and simply describe their own opinion about data. Arguments were often unsupported and asserted. In preparation for this type of question, centres are encouraged to give candidates regular opportunity to write extended essays in which they contrast and compare different perspectives or potential actions in response to an issue. In doing so, candidates need to analyse and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the reasons and evidence that supports and justifies the perspective or action.
notes.1a: All candidates correctly identified that the trend in worldwide use of the internet was increasing, from Source 1, and therefore gained the maximum of one mark for this question.
notes.1b: Almost all candidates were able to identify two benefits of digital technology from Source 2, and therefore gained the maximum of two marks for this question. Most candidates identified faster global communication, greater access to information and data, and sharing ideas globally.
notes.1c: Most candidates responded very well to this question and identified a benefit of digital technology which, in their opinion, was the most significant. Most candidates chose to discuss faster global communication and sharing ideas and perspectives. The most common justifications given by candidates related to issues of impact, included: • the number of people benefitting • the range of people affected e.g. different types of people or social groups • the degree of help given to people • impact on globalisation • the benefits to individuals, organisations and governments • economic benefits • impact on other aspects of society and social life generally, especially social media. The strongest responses provided clear explanation for the benefit and gave some reasons or evidence to support their judgements. Weaker responses often simply stated the benefit without explanation and tended to rely upon assertion without evidence or careful reasoning. Some candidates compared the significance of different benefits, but this was not necessary to gain full marks.
notes.1d: Many candidates responded very well to this question and could explain how the use of digital technology has important personal consequences. The explanations mainly related to the value of digital technology for individuals in their everyday lives, including for families and communities, especially for work, shopping and social media. These candidates demonstrated a clear understanding of the concept of ‘personal’. Candidates achieving at higher levels provided a clearly reasoned, credible and structured explanation. Candidates achieving at the lower levels tended to provide a limited explanation, or asserted opinion about technology in general, without reference to the personal dimension of the question.
notes.2a: Most candidates were able to evaluate the argument in Source 3 and assess how well the author supported the view that, ‘Data from digital technologies improves our lives.’. The strengths of the argument most often identified were: • uses the doctor as an expert to increase credibility • refers to a reputable organisation – the government • logical argument making the argument easy to follow • uses many relevant examples increases credibility • relevant evidence and reasons which are up to date. The weaknesses of the argument most often identified were: • few facts and statistics used to support the claim • emotive tone of language that may not be balanced • does not acknowledge counter arguments. The strongest responses provided clearly reasoned, credible and structured explanation of their evaluative points, usually discussing four or more distinct aspects of the source. Weaker responses often simply stated or asserted an opinion. Some weaker responses analysed and described the reasons and evidence within the source but did not evaluate or explain why the identified reason or type of evidence was a strength or weakness. For example, ‘A weakness is that the writer uses some assertion.’ This statement does not explain why assertion may not be strong evidence. A better response would be, ‘A weakness is that the writer relies upon assertion. This type of evidence is not strong because it is not supported with evidence. Therefore, we do not know if the statement is true. It has weak validity.’ Candidates should be encouraged to justify their opinion using the material in the source as evidence. This means being willing to quote from or summarise elements of the source.
notes.2b: Candidates who performed well in this question described several methods, sources of information and types of evidence that could be used to test the claim that, ‘Digital communication strengthens our relationships.’ The methods of testing the claim were carefully explained and clearly related to the claim. Candidates tended to describe interviews, surveys and questionnaires with people about the issue, often with different age groups in different places and cultures. Other methods included consultation with experts, psychologists and government officials. Most candidates suggested secondary research using sources from the internet. Many described the type of source that was likely to be reliable and free from bias or vested interest, for example from governments, NGOs and United Nations organisations. The strongest responses provided clearly reasoned, credible and structured explanations for their suggestions clearly and explicitly related to the claim being tested; weaker responses often simply stated a method or source of evidence but did not explain it fully or make the link to the claim being tested. A few candidates responded to the question by describing their opinion on the issue rather than describing how it could be researched. These responses gained very few, if any, marks. Candidates should be given regular opportunity to design research strategies to test claims as a regular part of their courses.
notes.3a: Most candidates correctly identified a fact from Source 4 and explained that a fact is something which can be verified or proven and is true or accurate. Most candidates were able to justify and explain their selection convincingly.
notes.3b: Most candidates were able to identify aspects of bias in Lar’s statement. These candidates showed understanding of bias as a tendency or prejudice for or against something, or an unbalanced approach to an issue, and not being prepared to consider counter arguments or other points of view. Most candidates were able to give several reasons why Lar’s statement might be biased. These included: • His experience of working for a data storage company may have influenced his viewpoint. • His argument is unbalanced showing very little consideration of other perspectives or counterarguments. • Use of exaggerated language and phrases, for example ‘data is extremely valuable’. • He only refers to positive aspects of data use. • His lack of much evidence. Centres are encouraged to teach candidates about bias in argument and the presentation of evidence and provide experience of using the term in the analysis and evaluation of sources, alongside other critical thinking concepts like value judgement, prediction, fact, vested interest and opinion.
notes.3c: Most candidates compared both statements explicitly, Kari’s and Lar’s, and discussed issues relating to evidence, language, knowledge claims and expertise. Some candidates also addressed the reasons and values within each statement. The strongest responses contained well supported, clearly explained judgements about the arguments with a clear assessment of each statement; this included coherent, structured evaluation of how well the argument worked with a range of evaluative points. These responses were usually balanced with a clear conclusion. The statements were also quoted explicitly and material from the statements was used directly in the response as evidence to support the candidate’s opinion. Weaker responses lacked supporting evidence and mainly asserted with little clarity of argument. These answers tended to focus on issues rather than reasons, language, knowledge claims, and evidence. There was little or no direct evaluation at the lowest levels of response. Centres are encouraged to give candidates frequent opportunity to evaluate sources during their courses. This should involve a consideration of the reasons and evidence used to support the argument or perspective in the source.
